The '''Adams Prize''' is a prize<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cambridgenetwork.co.uk/news/adams-prize-2002-3-winner-announced/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141023125424/http://www.cambridgenetwork.co.uk/news/adams-prize-2002-3-winner-announced/ |archive-date=23 October 2014 |title=Adams Prize 2002/3 winner announced – Cambridge Network}}</ref> awarded each year by the Faculty of Mathematics at [[St John's College, Cambridge|St John's College]] to a UK-based mathematician for distinguished research in mathematical sciences.

The prize is named after the mathematician [[John Couch Adams]] and was endowed by members of St John's College and approved by the senate of the university in 1848, to commemorate Adams' [[Discovery of Neptune|role]] in the discovery of the planet [[Neptune]]. Originally open only to Cambridge graduates, the current stipulation is that the mathematician must reside in the UK and be under forty years of age.<ref name="2012a">{{Cite web|url=http://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/news/4.html|title=Applications for Adams Prize 2012–13|date=23 February 2012|access-date=28 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141019231957/http://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/news/4.html|archive-date=19 October 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The Adams Prize is awarded in three parts: the first is paid directly to the candidate; another third is paid to the candidate's institution to fund research expenses; and the final third is paid on publication of a survey paper in the winner's field in a major mathematics journal.

The prize has been awarded to many well-known mathematicians, including
[[James Clerk Maxwell]] and [[W. V. D. Hodge|Sir William Hodge]]. The first female recipient, in 2002, was [[Susan Howson (mathematician)|Susan Howson]], then a lecturer at the [[University of Nottingham]], for her work on [[number theory]] and [[elliptic curves]].

==Subject area==
* 2015–16: Applied analysis<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/applications-adams-prize-2015-2016|title=Applications for Adams Prize 2015–2016|access-date=24 February 2016|archive-date=8 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190508023901/http://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/applications-adams-prize-2015-2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2016–17: Statistical analysis of big data<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/applications-adams-prize-2016-17|title=Applications for Adams Prize 2016–17 }}</ref>
* 2017–18: The mathematics of astronomy and cosmology<ref name=Adams1718>{{cite web|url=https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/adams-prize/winners-2017-18-announced|title=Adams prize winners 2017–18 announced|publisher=University of Cambridge|access-date= 6 September 2018}}</ref>
* 2018–19: The mathematics of networks<ref name=Adams1819>{{cite web|url=https://www.maths.cam.ac.uk/adams-prize|title=Adams prize2019|publisher=University of Cambridge|access-date= 19 September 2018}}</ref>
